organic: Prune branches to open the canopy for better airflow and faster leaf drying.
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to eliminate overwintering fungal spores.
Apply neem oil or sulfur-based organic fungicides at bud break and repeat every 7–10 days during wet weather.
chemical: Apply protective fungicides containing captan or mancozeb early in the season.
Alternate with systemic fungicides such as myclobutanil or difenoconazole to reduce resistance risk.
fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which promotes lush, scab-susceptible foliage.
Apply balanced NPK (e.g., 10-10-10) in early spring and consider a foliar urea spray after leaf drop to speed leaf decomposition.

organic: Prune out dead wood, cankers, and mummified fruit from the tree and orchard floor.
Sanitize pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol or diluted bleach between cuts.
Spray copper soap or Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide during early fruit set.
chemical: Apply captan, thiophanate-methyl, or strobilurin (azoxystrobin) sprays from petal fall through summer.
Follow label pre-harvest intervals strictly before picking.
fertilizer: Maintain adequate potassium and calcium nutrition to strengthen fruit skin and bark.
Use compost or slow-release balanced fertilizer rather than high-nitrogen quick-release feeds.

organic: Remove nearby eastern red cedar or juniper hosts within 1–2 miles if feasible, or prune orange galls off junipers in late winter.
Apply wettable sulfur or copper-based organic sprays starting at pink-bud stage through petal fall.
chemical: Apply myclobutanil, propiconazole, or mancozeb at 7–10 day intervals from tight cluster through second cover spray.
Rotate active ingredients to prevent fungal resistance.
fertilizer: Provide balanced spring NPK with micronutrients (zinc and boron) to support healthy leaf expansion.
Mulch the root zone with organic compost to reduce drought stress.

organic: No disease treatment needed; continue regular orchard sanitation and annual dormant pruning.
Monitor leaves weekly during damp spring weather for early signs of scab or rust.
chemical: No chemical fungicide application required.
fertilizer: Maintain standard seasonal balanced NPK fertilization based on soil test results.
Top-dress with well-rotted compost in spring to sustain soil organic matter.

organic: No treatment needed; maintain acidic pine-bark or sawdust mulch around the root zone.
Prune out old canes (>6 years) annually in late winter for airflow.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Use an acid-forming fertilizer (ammonium sulfate or ericaceous blend) to keep soil pH between 4.5 and 5.5.
Avoid nitrate-based fertilizers, which can damage blueberry roots.

organic: Apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oil, or wettable sulfur sprays at the first sign of white powdery patches.
Prune interior shoots to improve sunlight penetration and air circulation.
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day.
chemical: Apply myclobutanil, triflumizole, or quinoxyfen on a 10–14 day schedule during active shoot growth.
Rotate FRAC groups to delay fungicide resistance.
fertilizer: Limit summer nitrogen applications so late-season succulent shoots do not fuel mildew spread.
Maintain adequate potassium and calcium for stronger leaf cuticles.

organic: No treatment required; keep the canopy open and remove any suckers or fallen debris.
Water at the base rather than wetting foliage.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply a balanced fruit-tree fertilizer in early spring based on shoot growth and soil tests.
Supplement with compost mulch to conserve moisture.

organic: Rotate corn with non-host crops (such as soybeans or alfalfa) for 1–2 years.
Incorporate or remove infected corn residue after harvest to reduce inoculum.
Plant resistant maize hybrids in future seasons.
chemical: Apply foliar fungicides containing azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, or propiconazole at VT–R1 (tasseling/silking) if lesions reach the ear leaf.
fertilizer: Ensure adequate potassium (K) to improve stalk strength and foliar disease tolerance.
Side-dress nitrogen at V6 according to soil nitrate levels without over-applying.

organic: Select rust-resistant maize hybrids for next planting.
Monitor cool, humid periods (60–77°F) closely; biological sprays such as Bacillus-based products can help slow mild spread.
chemical: If infection is severe before silking on susceptible sweet corn or seed corn, apply mancozeb, azoxystrobin, or propiconazole.
fertilizer: Provide balanced nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium at planting to support vigorous early growth.
Avoid phosphorus deficiency, which delays maturity and extends susceptibility.

organic: Rotate away from corn for at least 1 year and till or shred infected crop residue.
Choose hybrids with Ht resistance genes when replanting.
chemical: Apply triazole or strobilurin fungicides (e.g., propiconazole + azoxystrobin) at early tasseling if upper leaves develop cigar-shaped lesions.
fertilizer: Maintain balanced N-P-K nutrition and adequate potassium to limit yield loss from premature leaf death.
Ensure proper plant spacing to reduce leaf wetness duration.

organic: No disease treatment needed; continue crop rotation and regular field scouting.
Keep weeds controlled to maintain airflow through rows.
chemical: No chemical fungicide required.
fertilizer: Follow split nitrogen application (starter at planting plus side-dress at V6) along with soil-tested P and K.
Include zinc if soil tests indicate micronutrient deficiency.

organic: Remove and destroy all mummified berries and infected tendrils during dormant pruning.
Use shoot thinning and leaf pulling around the fruit zone to speed drying.
Apply copper hydroxide or sulfur sprays early in the season (note: avoid sulfur on sulfur-sensitive grape varieties).
chemical: Apply mancozeb or captan from 6-inch shoot growth through bloom, followed by myclobutanil or azoxystrobin if wet weather persists.
fertilizer: Apply moderate, balanced vine nutrition (low-to-moderate nitrogen) to prevent overly dense canopies.
Ensure adequate potassium and magnesium for fruit quality.

organic: Prune out symptomatic canes or perform trunk renewal during dry weather only.
Protect fresh pruning wounds with Trichoderma-based biological wound sealants.
Remove and burn severely declining vines to stop trunk-fungus spread.
chemical: No curative foliar fungicide exists for established Esca; apply protective pruning-wound paste (e.g., thiophanate-methyl or pyraclostrobin wound protectants) immediately after pruning.
fertilizer: Avoid water and nutrient stress with steady drip irrigation and organic compost.
Supply balanced potassium and micronutrients rather than heavy nitrogen.

organic: Remove heavily spotted lower leaves and collect fallen leaf litter after harvest.
Spray fixed copper or Bordeaux mixture when spots first appear.
chemical: Apply mancozeb, captan, or copper oxychloride at 10–14 day intervals during humid weather.
fertilizer: Provide balanced NPK and potassium supplements to sustain leaf longevity through berry ripening.
Avoid excess nitrogen that encourages dense, shaded foliage.

organic: No treatment required; continue canopy management and seasonal pruning for airflow.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply light spring compost or balanced NPK according to petiole/soil analysis.
Supplement boron and zinc prior to bloom if tests show low levels.

organic: Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector using horticultural oils, insecticidal soap, or neem oil.
Remove and destroy severely infected trees to protect surrounding healthy citrus.
chemical: No chemical cure exists for Citrus Greening (HLB) bacteria; manage psyllid vectors with registered systemic or foliar insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid or spinetoram) per local extension rules.
fertilizer: Apply frequent, small doses of controlled-release NPK plus enhanced foliar micronutrients (zinc, manganese, iron, boron, magnesium) to prolong tree productivity.
Maintain slightly acidic soil pH (6.0–6.5) for optimal nutrient uptake.

organic: Apply fixed copper sprays at leaf drop in autumn and again at delayed dormant bud swell.
Prune to maintain an open vase canopy and plant windbreaks to reduce wind-driven leaf abrasion.
chemical: Apply oxytetracycline (antibiotic) or low-rate copper sprays during shuck split through early cover sprays, rotating carefully to minimize phytotoxicity.
fertilizer: Avoid excessive nitrogen, which causes tender growth vulnerable to bacterial entry.
Maintain balanced potassium and calcium levels.

organic: No treatment needed; maintain open-center pruning and remove any mummified fruit in winter.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply balanced stone-fruit fertilizer in early spring based on prior year's shoot growth.
Mulch around the drip line while keeping mulch away from the trunk.

organic: Remove and destroy symptomatic leaves or severely infected plants immediately.
Avoid working in the field when foliage is wet and switch from overhead sprinklers to drip irrigation.
Spray fixed copper mixed with a biological (Bacillus amyloliquefaciens) weekly.
chemical: Apply copper hydroxide or copper octanoate tank-mixed with mancozeb (where registered) on a 7-day preventive schedule.
fertilizer: Use balanced N-P-K with supplemental calcium (calcium nitrate) to strengthen cell walls.
Avoid high nitrogen bursts that create soft, infection-prone tissue.

organic: No treatment required; rotate peppers away from tomatoes and eggplants every 3 years.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Provide balanced fertilizer (e.g., 5-10-10 or 10-10-10) plus calcium to prevent blossom-end rot.
Side-dress lightly once fruits begin setting.

organic: Remove lower infected leaves and mulch soil to prevent rain-splash of spores.
Apply copper-based fungicide or Bacillus subtilis early when target-like concentric rings appear.
Practice a 3-year crop rotation out of solanaceous crops.
chemical: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin/difenoconazole every 7–10 days during warm, humid weather.
fertilizer: Maintain steady nitrogen and potassium nutrition—early blight attacks nitrogen-stressed or aging plants fastest.
Avoid late-season nutrient starvation by side-dressing at hilling.

organic: Remove and bag infected plants immediately; do not compost diseased foliage.
Apply protective copper hydroxide sprays before cool, wet weather arrives.
Hill soil well over tubers and wait 2 weeks after vine kill before harvesting.
chemical: Apply systemic + protectant late-blight fungicides immediately (e.g., chlorothalonil, mancozeb, fluopicolide, or cymoxanil-based products) on a strict 5–7 day schedule.
fertilizer: Provide balanced P and K for tuber development while avoiding excessive late nitrogen that delays vine maturity.
Ensure well-drained soil to avoid waterlogging.

organic: No disease treatment needed; keep tubers well hilled and inspect lower leaves weekly.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply phosphorus and potassium at planting with moderate split nitrogen at emergence and hilling.
Maintain slightly acidic soil pH (5.5–6.5) to prevent scab.

organic: No treatment needed; thin floricanes after harvest to maintain air circulation and narrow row widths.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply balanced 10-10-10 or composted manure in early spring before new cane growth begins.
Ensure good drainage to prevent root rot.

organic: No treatment needed; continue crop rotation and scout periodically for pods and foliage.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Inoculate seeds with Bradyrhizobium japonicum at planting to support biological nitrogen fixation.
Supply phosphorus, potassium, and sulfur based on soil test recommendations.

organic: Spray potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or sulfur (avoid sulfur above 85°F/30°C to prevent leaf burn).
Remove heavily whitened older leaves and space plants well for airflow.
Water at soil level early in the morning.
chemical: Apply chlorothalonil, myclobutanil, or triflumizole alternating modes of action every 7–10 days.
fertilizer: Maintain balanced NPK and adequate potassium during fruiting.
Avoid excessive nitrogen that produces overly shaded, tender vines.

organic: Remove and destroy scorched outer leaves and renovate beds after harvest.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry.
Apply copper soap or organic sulfur preventively in cool, wet spring weather.
chemical: Apply captan or myclobutanil from early spring growth through fruit set as needed.
fertilizer: Feed lightly after harvest (renovation) rather than heavy early-spring nitrogen, which increases soft foliage and rot.
Ensure adequate potassium for runner and crown resilience.

organic: No treatment needed; keep straw mulch under berries and renovate beds annually after fruiting.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply balanced fertilizer at renovation in late summer and light spring feeding if vigor is low.
Maintain soil pH between 5.8 and 6.5.

organic: Prune away lower spotted leaves using sanitized shears and avoid handling plants when wet.
Mulch soil to prevent splash dispersal and switch to drip irrigation.
Apply fixed copper plus a Bacillus-based bio-fungicide every 7 days.
chemical: Apply copper hydroxide combined with mancozeb (where permitted) on a 7-day preventive schedule.
fertilizer: Provide steady balanced NPK with supplemental calcium nitrate to strengthen plant tissues.
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen.

organic: Prune off lower leaves up to 12 inches from the soil and stake/cage plants for airflow.
Apply straw or plastic mulch to block soil-borne spores from splashing onto leaves.
Spray copper fungicide, neem oil, or Bacillus subtilis weekly.
chemical: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin every 7–10 days starting when lower leaves show concentric rings.
fertilizer: Ensure adequate nitrogen and potassium—deficient tomato plants succumb much faster to Early Blight.
Side-dress with compost or balanced tomato feed at first fruit set.

organic: Immediately pull and bag infected plants—do not compost them, as spores spread rapidly by wind.
Apply preventive copper sprays ahead of cool, rainy weather.
Provide wide spacing and avoid overhead watering.
chemical: Apply protective and systemic late-blight fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or mandipropamid/fluopicolide) immediately every 5–7 days.
fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition (moderate nitrogen, good potassium and calcium) and well-drained soil.
Avoid lush, overly dense foliage from excess nitrogen.

organic: Increase greenhouse or tunnel ventilation and reduce relative humidity below 85%.
Prune lower leaves and suckers to maximize airflow; water only at the soil surface.
Apply potassium bicarbonate or copper sprays at first yellow upper-leaf spots.
chemical: Apply chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or difenoconazole thoroughly to leaf undersides where olive-green mold grows.
fertilizer: Keep calcium and potassium balanced and avoid excess nitrogen that creates dense canopies.
Space irrigation early in the day so humidity drops before nightfall.

organic: Remove spotted lower leaves immediately and dispose of them away from the garden.
Mulch heavily around plant bases and clean/sanitize tomato stakes before reuse.
Apply copper octanoate or potassium bicarbonate weekly during wet weather.
chemical: Apply chlorothalonil or mancozeb every 7–10 days from first appearance of small circular spots with dark margins.
fertilizer: Maintain consistent watering and balanced NPK + calcium feeding to sustain healthy upper foliage.
Avoid splashing soil onto stems when fertilizing.

organic: Spray plants—especially leaf undersides—with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites and webbing.
Apply insecticidal soap, neem oil, or horticultural oil every 5–7 days to target newly hatched nymphs.
Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) in enclosed/greenhouse setups.
chemical: Apply targeted miticides/acaricides such as abamectin, bifenazate, or spiromesifen, rotating classes to avoid resistance (avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroids that kill natural predators).
fertilizer: Avoid drought stress and excessive quick-release nitrogen, both of which accelerate mite reproduction.
Keep soil evenly moist and use balanced slow-release nutrients.

organic: Prune lower leaves and increase spacing/staking to improve airflow through the lower canopy.
Apply copper-based organic sprays or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens at early symptom onset.
chemical: Apply chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin, or difenoconazole every 7–10 days during warm, humid conditions.
fertilizer: Supply balanced NPK with adequate potassium and calcium to strengthen foliage and fruit skin.
Avoid waterlogging and overhead watering.

organic: Rogue (remove and bag) infected plants early so whiteflies cannot spread the virus further.
Use yellow sticky traps, fine insect netting, and neem oil or insecticidal soap to suppress silverleaf whiteflies.
chemical: No chemical cure exists for viral infection; control whitefly vectors with targeted insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid, pyriproxyfen, or acetamiprid) and plant TYLCV-resistant varieties next season.
fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition and steady irrigation for remaining healthy plants; do not over-feed infected plants with nitrogen, which attracts whiteflies.

organic: Remove and destroy infected plants promptly—do not compost them.
Wash hands with soap and sanitize tools in 10% milk or trisodium phosphate solution before touching healthy tomatoes (tobacco products can also transmit TMV).
chemical: No chemical treatment cures Tomato Mosaic Virus; focus strictly on sanitation, weed host removal, and planting TMV-resistant varieties.
fertilizer: Support healthy surrounding plants with balanced NPK and micronutrients while avoiding mechanical damage during side-dressing.

organic: No disease treatment needed; maintain staking, lower-leaf pruning, and mulch around the base.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.
fertilizer: Apply balanced tomato fertilizer (higher phosphorus and potassium once flowering starts) plus calcium to prevent blossom-end rot.
Water consistently at the base.
